spans.note: title and Executive Summary heading with blank lines

spans.assertion: the analysis used a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads across four European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain) from the 2012-2013 season to test whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: after adjusting for position, physical characteristics, league, and game exposure, the estimated risk difference was 0.078 percentage points higher for dark-skinned vs light-skinned players (95% CI -0.065 to 0.243 pp, p=0.296)
the risk difference was not statistically significant at the α=0.05 level

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis
the observed difference is small in magnitude
the observed difference is not statistically significant
the confidence interval includes zero and negative values, indicating a possible advantage for dark-skinned players

spans.note: section break and heading for Section 1

spans.assertion: the adjusted risk difference (dark vs light skin) is 0.078 percentage points, 95% CI [-0.065, 0.243] pp, two-sided p=0.296
the p-value indicates the result is not significant at α=0.05

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: adjusted probability of a red card is 0.86% for dark-skinned players and 0.78% for light-skinned players, yielding the 0.078pp risk difference
the difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero
the 95% CI is wide and includes negative values, indicating substantial uncertainty and the possibility of no effect or a protective effect

spans.note: section break and heading for Section 2

spans.assertion: the adjusted odds ratio (dark vs light skin) is 1.101, 95% CI [0.918, 1.321], p=0.300

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: odds of a red card are about 10% higher for dark-skinned players than light-skinned players
this odds difference is not statistically significant
the CI includes the null value of 1.0, indicating no reliable evidence of differential treatment

spans.note: section break and headings for Section 3 and Unit of Analysis

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis chosen was the player-referee dyad, defined as all encounters between a specific player and specific referee
the analytical sample contains 115,603 dyads
the sample contains 1,419 unique players
the sample contains 2,904 unique referees
mean games per dyad is 3.03 (SD 3.64, range 1-47)

spans.note: blank line and Skin Tone Measurement heading

spans.assertion: skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters coding player photos on a 5-point scale normalized to 0-1
inter-rater correlation was 0.923, described as excellent agreement
exact rater agreement was 76.8%, and agreement within one category was 99.9%
players were categorized into three skin-tone groups using cutoffs: light (0.00-0.25), medium (0.375-0.625), dark (0.75-1.00)
category counts were: light 83,655 dyads (72.4%), medium 13,770 dyads (11.9%), dark 18,178 dyads (15.7%)

spans.note: blank line and Outcome Variable heading

spans.assertion: the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of any red card in the player-referee dyad
red card prevalence was 1.26% of dyads (1,455 of 115,603)
unadjusted red card rates by skin tone were: light 1.21%, medium 1.46%, dark 1.31%

spans.note: blank line and Covariates Included heading

spans.assertion: the model adjusted for four confounders: log-transformed game exposure, player position (4 categories), standardized height and weight, and league country (4 categories)
defenders received red cards at a higher rate (1.53%) than other positions
height (mean 182.2cm, SD 6.9) and weight (mean 76.5kg, SD 7.2) were standardized before inclusion

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: position was included because defensive players have more physical confrontations and thus higher red card risk
position distribution differed by skin tone: dark-skinned players were more likely to be forwards and less likely to be goalkeepers
physical characteristics were included to control for playing-style correlates
league country was included to account for cross-national differences in referee strictness
game exposure was included as essential to account for varying opportunities for red cards

spans.note: blank line and Exclusions heading

spans.assertion: 21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone data (players without profile photos or uncodable by raters)
9,018 dyads were excluded for missing covariate data, primarily missing position (8,461)
the final analytical sample was 115,603 dyads, 79.2% of the original dataset

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: skin-tone missingness was assessed as likely missing completely at random with respect to referee behavior, though potentially related to player prominence
a complete-case analysis was judged reasonable, with the caveat that results apply only to the subset of players with photos

spans.note: blank line and Statistical Model heading

spans.assertion: a logistic regression model with logit link was fit using maximum likelihood estimation
standard errors were clustered by player to account for within-player correlation across referees
a sensitivity analysis was also run clustering standard errors by referee

spans.note: blank line and Standard Error and Inference Approach heading

spans.assertion: standard errors were clustered by player, using 1,419 clusters
confidence intervals were calculated using a parametric bootstrap with 10,000 draws from the estimated coefficient distribution
two-sided hypothesis tests at α=0.05 were used for p-values
the risk difference was calculated as marginal effects at covariate means, comparing predicted probabilities for dark vs light skin with other variables held constant

spans.note: blank line and Adjustment Strategy heading

spans.assertion: the regression model included all covariates simultaneously
the adjusted risk difference was computed by predicting probabilities under two counterfactual scenarios (all players dark skin vs all players light skin, at average covariates)

spans.note: section break and Conclusion heading

spans.assertion: the stated conclusion is that the hypothesis is not supported

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis
the point estimate suggests a small positive association of 0.078 percentage points

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the finding is not statistically significant (p=0.296), so chance cannot be ruled out as the explanation
the effect is small in magnitude, less than 0.1 percentage point against a baseline risk of about 0.8%
the finding is highly uncertain, with the 95% CI ranging from a 0.065pp advantage to a 0.243pp disadvantage for dark-skinned players

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the adjusted odds ratio of 1.10, with a CI including the null value 1.0, similarly shows no reliable evidence of bias

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: even if accurate, a 0.078pp difference is practically negligible, equating to about 0.078 extra red cards per 100 games for a player

spans.note: section break, Limitations heading, and Unit of Analysis subheading

spans.assertion: player-referee dyads rather than individual games were used as the unit of analysis, a choice dictated by the data structure
using dyads as the unit reduces noise from single-game variation
using dyads aggregates across time and contexts, potentially masking within-dyad heterogeneity
total games per dyad was controlled for as a mitigation for the unit-of-analysis limitation
results were robust in a player-level sensitivity analysis

spans.note: blank line and Missing Data heading

spans.assertion: approximately 21% of dyads lacked skin tone data due to players without photos
an additional 7% of dyads were excluded due to missing covariates

spans.note: general caveat that results may not generalize if players without photos differ systematically in referee treatment

spans.assertion: missingness was assessed as likely related to player prominence rather than skin-tone/referee interactions, so bias is judged probably minimal

spans.note: blank line and Skin Tone Measurement subheading

spans.assertion: coding skin tone from photos by raters is acknowledged to introduce measurement error
high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923) and the use of multiple raters are said to reduce this bias
raters coding the photos were blind to the research question, though photos may not fully capture true skin tone due to lighting or photo quality
measurement error is claimed to typically bias results toward the null, so the true effect is judged unlikely to be larger

spans.note: blank line and Confounding heading

spans.assertion: the analysis controlled for position, physical characteristics, league, and exposure, but could not rule out residual confounding
playing style (aggressiveness) was not controlled for as a potential confounder linking skin tone and red cards
team quality was not controlled for as a potential confounder of skin tone distribution and referee scrutiny
individual referee characteristics/bias could not be controlled for due to the data structure
players' historical disciplinary reputation was not controlled for
the most plausible confounders were included as a mitigation
referee-country fixed effects were tested in a sensitivity analysis

spans.note: blank line and Multiple Comparisons heading

spans.assertion: the analysis focused on a single primary hypothesis and estimand, so multiple-testing concerns are minimal

spans.note: blank line and Ecological Fallacy heading
general caveat that aggregate results could mask referee-specific or context-specific bias in either direction
blank line and Statistical Power heading

spans.assertion: the study is claimed to have >99% power to detect a risk difference of 0.2pp or larger, so the null finding is not attributed to insufficient power

spans.note: blank line and Temporal and Geographic Generalizability heading
caveats that findings are limited to the 2012-2013 season, four European leagues, and male players, and may not generalize
section break, Key Assumptions heading, and Assumption 1 subheading

spans.assertion: logistic regression was assumed appropriate for the binary red-card outcome
the outcome is binary and the logit link is described as standard, offered as verification of the modeling assumption
no higher-order interactions were tested, leaving the log-linear predictor/log-odds assumption unverified

spans.note: blank line and Assumption 2 subheading

spans.assertion: dyads were assumed independent within player clusters
clustering standard errors by player was used to account for within-player correlation, offered as verification of the independence assumption
a sensitivity check clustering by referee instead was also run and gave consistent results

spans.note: blank line and Assumption 3 subheading

spans.assertion: the included covariates were assumed to capture all common causes of skin tone and red card risk
the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption cannot be directly tested, but all available plausible confounders were included
position and league are judged strong confounders, so remaining confounding bias is judged likely small

spans.note: blank line and Assumption 4 (Positivity) subheading

spans.assertion: all skin tone categories were assumed to be represented across covariate strata
the large sample was verified to have good overlap with no empty cells

spans.note: blank line and Assumption 5 (No Selection Bias) subheading

spans.assertion: missing data was assumed not to induce bias
missingness was judged likely unrelated to referee bias, making complete-case analysis appropriate

spans.note: blank line and Assumption 6 (Measurement Validity) subheading

spans.assertion: rater-coded skin tone was assumed to validly capture referee perceptions
raters viewed photos rather than live players, creating a possible mismatch with referees' actual perceptions
high inter-rater reliability is cited as suggesting consistent measurement despite this limitation

spans.note: section break, Sensitivity Analyses heading, and Sensitivity Analysis 1 subheading

spans.assertion: the main analysis clustered standard errors by player
a sensitivity analysis clustered standard errors by referee instead (2,904 clusters)
under referee-clustered SEs the risk difference was found to be 0.079pp (95% CI -0.045 to 0.208pp, p=0.212)
the referee-clustered CI was slightly narrower but led to the same substantive conclusion
results were judged robust to the clustering choice, with no evidence of bias under either specification

spans.note: blank line and Sensitivity Analysis 2 subheading

spans.assertion: an alternative analysis used individual players (N=1,419) rather than dyads as the unit of analysis
for this alternative analysis the outcome was defined as a continuous red-card rate per game
the player-level analysis found a mean rate difference of 0.058pp, Welch's t-test p=0.205, and Mann-Whitney U p=0.285
the player-level analysis is interpreted as a consistent null finding

spans.note: blank line and Summary of Robustness subheading

spans.assertion: all sensitivity analyses are summarized as consistent, showing no significant difference, with point estimates ranging 0.058-0.079pp and all p-values >0.20

spans.note: section break, Supplementary Findings heading, and Medium Skin Tone subheading

spans.assertion: the medium skin tone category showed a coefficient of 0.174 (SE=0.091, p=0.056)
this result is described as borderline significant, suggesting a possible non-linear relationship
the medium skin tone finding is flagged as post-hoc and not pre-specified in the hypothesis

spans.note: blank line and Position Effects subheading

spans.assertion: position was strongly associated with red card risk: defenders had the highest risk, forwards had 37% lower odds (p<0.001), goalkeepers 26% lower odds (p=0.008), and midfielders 41% lower odds (p<0.001)

spans.note: blank line and League Effects subheading

spans.assertion: significant variation across leagues was found: France and Spain had higher red card rates than England, and Germany had lower rates than England

spans.note: section break and Methodological Strengths heading

spans.assertion: the large sample size (>115,000 dyads) is cited as providing excellent statistical power
red cards are characterized as a discrete, objectively recorded outcome
skin-tone exposure measurement via independent raters with high reliability is cited as valid
logistic regression with clustered SE and marginal effects is described as an appropriate statistical method
all code, data, and decisions are claimed to be documented (transparency)
findings are described as consistent across multiple specifications and sensitivity analyses
confounder control is described as comprehensive, adjusting for key alternative explanations

spans.note: section break and Overall Assessment heading

spans.assertion: the overall assessment is that there is no evidence of referee bias against dark-skinned players after adjusting for position, physical characteristics, league, and exposure
the CI includes zero, indicating the data are consistent with no bias

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the overall finding is stated as no reliable, generalizable evidence of skin-tone bias, while acknowledging the analysis cannot rule out small or context-specific effects

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: hypothesis status is declared NOT SUPPORTED

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the null hypothesis of no difference cannot be rejected; the data do not sufficiently support elevated red-card risk for dark-skinned players due to referee bias

spans.note: section break and Technical Note: Reproducibility heading

spans.assertion: the analysis was conducted in Python 3.11 using pandas 2.x, numpy 1.x, statsmodels 0.14, and scipy 1.x
the random seed was set to 42 for all bootstrap procedures
all analyses are claimed to be fully reproducible via the provided final_analysis.py code file
